900.bp: When a new user shows up with almost no purchase history, a recommendation system has almost nothing to learn from. The real goal is to quickly suggest items they might like using only a handful of their first interactions, while the system keeps evolving as millions of new users arrive with their own preference patterns.
900.wh: The tension is between two opposing forces: you need a general model that works for anyone (trained on many past users), but you also need to adapt that model to each person's unique tastes. As preferences shift over time and new users continuously arrive, the old general model gets stale; but retraining from scratch wastes everything you learned before.
900.ap: The paper proposes a method that splits the learning into two paths working together. One path preserves the broad patterns of preference across all users (the general model). The other path learns to adjust those patterns for each new user as they arrive and show their preferences over time. When new users arrive in batches, the system replays examples from past batches to prevent the general model from forgetting, while a separate mechanism picks which old examples to replay so they stay relevant.
900.ww: This works because human preferences do have common threads (many people like popular items), but also idiosyncratic differences. By keeping both the shared knowledge and the personalized tweaks separate, the model can adapt quickly to a new person without destroying what works for everyone else. Replaying past examples prevents catastrophic forgetting—the problem where a neural network forgets old lessons when learning new ones.
900.po: The system can now recommend items to brand-new users faster and more accurately as preferences shift over time. The paper shows this approach outperforms methods that either stick rigidly to one general model or methods that learn each user entirely from scratch, by preserving the best of both strategies.

901.bp: Large language models are now being used as agents that can call external tools—search engines, calculators, APIs, databases—to solve real problems. The hard part is teaching the model which tool to use for which situation, especially when the toolset is messy, incomplete, or keeps changing.
901.wh: Real-world training data is a mess: some tools are used way more often than others (long-tail distribution), some specialized tools have almost no examples, some instructions directly contradict available tools, and some examples in the training set are just wrong or partially correct. Standard supervised learning treats all examples equally, but if you learn from bad examples, the model learns bad habits.
901.ap: The paper proposes TOOL-CURE, which uses reinforcement learning—a method where the model learns from rewards instead of direct labels. Instead of treating all training examples the same, they organize examples into easy ones first (foundational skills) then harder ones (edge cases), teaching the model gradually like you'd teach a person. They also add a filter to spot and skip low-quality training examples—ones that look wrong, partially right, or just noisy.
901.ww: Reinforcement learning works here because the model can learn 'what happens if I pick this tool' by seeing real outcomes, rather than blindly copying labeled examples. Curriculum learning (easy-to-hard progression) prevents the model from getting confused by hard cases before it masters the basics. Filtering noisy examples removes misleading signals that would push the model in the wrong direction.
901.po: The model learns to pick the right tool even for specialized, rare cases and adapts when the toolset changes. Testing shows the method handles imbalanced, noisy, and conflicting training data much better than standard supervised learning, and produces more stable training than vanilla reinforcement learning.

902.bp: When earthquakes, protests, or disease outbreaks happen, people post about them online with photos and text. Automatically detecting these real-world events from social media is crucial for emergency response and public safety, but you have to work with whatever messy, unstructured data appears in the wild.
902.wh: The old way required someone to hand-label thousands of posts as 'earthquake' or 'protest'—expensive and impossible to scale to all event types. Also, if you train a model on predefined event categories (say, 10 types), it fails when event type 11 happens in the real world. You can't predict how many event types exist before they occur.
902.ap: The paper proposes a label-free approach: instead of needing labeled examples, they use a large language model to look at raw image-text pairs and automatically enrich them with descriptions. For each post, they ask the model 'what's the event theme, event type, and image details' and construct enriched versions. They then use a two-stream network to learn which posts are related to each other (similar images and text go together) without any hand-crafted labels.
902.ww: This works because posts about the same real-world event naturally share visual and textual patterns even if you've never labeled them before. A language model can reason about events from general knowledge without needing specific training. By learning which things are similar (self-supervised learning), the model naturally groups posts by underlying event, discovering the event types organically instead of guessing them upfront.
902.po: The system can now detect new event types it has never seen before, and it works without requiring expensive hand-labeled datasets. The method handles the dynamic, open-ended nature of social media where new events constantly emerge.

903.bp: Online ads platforms need to predict whether a user will complete a purchase (conversion rate prediction) so they can price ads and rank them. But sales behavior changes wildly during big sales events like Black Friday or 618 Shopping Day—millions of extra buyers, changed habits, completely different patterns.
903.wh: Models trained on normal days fail catastrophically during sales events because the patterns are so different. Retraining from scratch each time wastes months of learning from normal days. The trick is knowing which parts of what you learned still apply (stable patterns everyone follows) versus which parts need to flip for the event (event-specific behavior).
903.ap: The paper proposes a split-brain approach: one part of the model learns stable, event-independent patterns from raw user data. Another part is an event-aware specialist that adjusts predictions for the current situation. They align the stable part across normal days and sale days so the features match up cleanly. They also build a 'gate' mechanism that decides how much to trust the specialist versus the stable part, adapting per user and per prediction.
903.ww: This works because some user behavior is truly universal (people who normally buy often still buy), while other behavior is purely event-dependent (new buyers show up during sales). By splitting the model, you get stable knowledge transfer (the stable part) combined with situational awareness (the specialist). Alignment ensures the model speaks the same language on normal and event days.
903.po: Deployed on a real short-video ad platform during a major sale event, the system improved conversion rate predictions by 7.5% and platform revenue by 4.3%, while barely increasing model size or latency. The approach handles the periodic swings in user behavior that break traditional models.

904.bp: Large e-commerce recommendation systems use multiple separate search models in parallel to get fast, diverse suggestions: one model finds popular items, one finds items similar to what you've bought, one finds trending items, etc. Combining them is efficient, but it risks showing redundant suggestions because some results appear in multiple models.
904.wh: If all the separate models return similar results, showing users every overlap wastes ranking slots. You want new, non-redundant results, but you can't just ask models to avoid previous results—they were designed independently. The naive fix of filtering duplicates is too blunt and loses useful information.
904.ap: The paper proposes focusing on results that only the new model found—samples that didn't appear in previous models. They call this 'incremental' samples. They then build a separate learning system trained to rank and emphasize these incremental samples. A second mechanism ensures these samples also have high real-world value (users will actually interact with them), not just technical uniqueness.
904.ww: This works because redundancy is real waste—if five models all return the same top item, showing it five times doesn't help. By explicitly optimizing for what's new rather than just relevant, you use ranking slots more efficiently. Measuring real exposure probability ensures the model doesn't just pick obscure samples; it picks samples that are both new and valuable.
904.po: Deployed on Taobao's homepage recommendations, the system increased transaction count by 1% just by better balancing novelty and value. It shows that treating multi-model retrieval as an incremental learning problem, rather than just aggregation, improves real business outcomes.

905.bp: A bookstore wants to recommend books: it has a book database but sparse reviews within each store's local inventory. By looking at the main store's reviews (books, ratings) plus a small store's inventory, it might transfer knowledge about which books sell well. But 'popular in the main store' might mean something completely different in a niche store.
905.wh: Naive transfer assumes knowledge from one domain applies to all others—'this book is good' should mean the same everywhere. But it doesn't. A business book might be niche and slow-selling in a used bookstore but hit hard in a corporate setting. Blind transfer can actually make recommendations worse because you're forcing concepts across incompatible contexts.
905.ap: The paper builds a graph where items connect to topics (extracted from book descriptions), and topics connect to words. They then classify each word as 'this word means something specific to one domain,' 'shared across all domains,' or 'universal meaning independent of domain.' Using this graph structure, the model learns item representations that separate out the domain-specific noise from universal signals.
905.ww: This works because language is ambiguous: the word 'novel' means different things in literary fiction versus tech conferences. By explicitly disentangling these meanings, the model can transfer the universal signal ('these topics matter') without importing domain-specific baggage. A word's frequency across domains reveals which bucket it belongs to.
905.po: The system predicts ratings and rankings better across different store types because it avoids negative transfer—learning bad patterns from one domain. It shows that simple transfer fails for recommendations, but careful disentanglement succeeds.

906.bp: In a social network, some people are more influential than others—they know more people, their opinions spread further. 'Katz centrality' is a math way to measure this influence. Computing it exactly requires huge matrix operations that take forever on billion-node networks.
906.wh: The exact formula involves matrix powers that grow exponentially with network size. For large graphs, exact computation is prohibitively expensive—cubic time complexity means trillions of operations. Existing approximation methods exist but don't parallelize well, so they can't harness modern multi-processor computers.
906.ap: The paper proposes two Monte Carlo algorithms—methods that use random sampling instead of exact calculation. The algorithms simulate random walks through the network (imagine dropping a ball on a node and watching it bounce to random neighbors). After many simulated walks, you count how often the ball lands on each node; that count approximates its influence.
906.ww: Random walks converge to the true centrality distribution through the law of large numbers—if you simulate enough walks, the frequency of landing on a node approaches its true importance. Monte Carlo is highly parallelizable because thousands of random walks can run independently on different processors. You trade a little accuracy for massive speed.
906.po: The algorithm runs 100 to 1000 times faster than exact methods while maintaining high accuracy in ranking the most influential nodes. The approach scales to billion-node networks on modern parallel hardware.

907.bp: When you search for shoes on Amazon, you no longer see a simple list—you see a grid of images, filter panels on the side, brand suggestions, price ranges. Ranking these elements matters because layout and visual design shape which items users notice and buy. But old ranking systems assume a vertical list, not this complex 2D layout.
907.wh: Position bias (click-through depends on where an item sits) isn't linear anymore—the top-left corner item and middle item have different effects. Also, companies want long-term happier customers, not just today's clicks. But measuring long-term satisfaction is hard because results take weeks (did this user come back? buy again?), and you can't easily trace which item caused which future behavior.
907.ap: The paper proposes a framework that models how item relevance, 2D position, and visual design all interact. They use causal inference to measure long-term satisfaction from observational data (quasi-experiments: 'when we showed item X in position Y, what happened to users over 14 days'). They then test the full layout-aware model with real A/B testing on live Amazon traffic.
907.ww: This works because the right item in the wrong spot on the page is nearly invisible, while the wrong item in the perfect spot gets clicked. By modeling layout explicitly, you can find the true ranking. Causal inference extracts long-term signals from observational data without waiting months for outcomes, letting you optimize faster.
907.po: The system improved brand relevance (a customer experience metric) by 1.86% and revenue by 0.05% on live e-commerce search. It shows that page layout matters as much as item ranking, and measuring long-term impact unlocks better optimization.

908.bp: Recommendation systems that generate text (like generating a playlist description or explaining why something was recommended) can produce better results with longer user history. But longer history means more computation—slower real-time response, higher server costs, less room for other features.
908.wh: A user's purchase history might have 500 items. Feeding all 500 items into a language model is expensive. You could truncate to the last 50, but then you lose signal about long-term interests. You want to compress without losing meaning.
908.ap: The paper proposes using item categories (which already exist in the database) to compress history. Instead of remembering 'bought phone, bought charger, bought screen protector, bought phone stand,' you remember 'bought 4 phone accessories.' By grouping items by category and summarizing counts, you retain the signal (this person likes phone accessories) in a fraction of the space.
908.ww: This works because the pattern 'bought many phone accessories' captures the user's interest better than each individual item. Item categories are already meaningful human-defined groups, so you're not throwing away information that matters. The model still sees the distribution across categories, which is what drives recommendation.
908.po: The method achieves 6 times faster inference and 39% higher recommendation accuracy at the same computational cost as a longer history baseline. It proves that smart compression using existing metadata (categories) outperforms longer, denser sequences.

909.bp: Imagine you run a network of hospitals and want to estimate: if we give this patient a new treatment, how much will it help? This is hard in a network because patients see each other (information spreads), and which patients get treatment might depend on hidden factors like social connections or unobserved wealth.
909.wh: Networks create two problems: (1) Confounding: unmeasured factors like wealth influence both whether someone gets treatment and their outcome, making it hard to separate treatment effect from those hidden factors. (2) Spillover: if your friend gets treatment, it might affect you (they share advice, reduce disease spread). You can't just look at treated versus untreated; the untreated group is contaminated by spillover.
909.ap: The paper proposes learning three separate latent factors for each person: one that influences treatment assignment (instrumental factor), one that's a confounding variable, and one that adjusts outcomes. They learn these by looking at network structure (friends reveal information patterns), applying reweighting (up-weight people who look like they shouldn't have received treatment but did), and adding regularization constraints that ensure the three factors are actually separate.
909.ww: This works because hidden factors often have distinct roles. Wealth influences both treatment and outcome (confounder), but a doctor's belief in a treatment influences who gets it without directly affecting outcome (instrument). By learning these roles separately with network structure guiding the learning, you can identify which variation is pure treatment effect versus confounding or spillover.
909.po: The method produces better estimates of individual treatment effects in networked settings. Theory guarantees the latent factors are identifiable, and experiments on synthetic and real data show the approach outperforms methods that ignore network structure or hide confounding.

910.bp: Manufacturing plants, power grids, and hospitals collect thousands of sensors continuously (temperature, pressure, voltage)—a multivariate time series. When something breaks, you see anomalies: a sudden temperature spike, an unusual pressure pattern. But detecting anomalies is hard because normal operation has natural variation.
910.wh: Most anomaly detectors are trained to predict all sensor streams simultaneously—if you're forecasting 100 sensors, the model spreads its effort across all 100. But some sensors are more important than others, and the model's error gets diluted across all streams. You want focused detection on the sensors that matter most.
910.ap: The paper proposes focusing anomaly detection on one important sensor at a time. For that target sensor, you use neighboring sensors with similar patterns as additional input features (since they provide context). The model learns to predict only the target sensor, concentrating all its predictive power on that one stream.
910.ww: This works because narrowing focus reduces dilution. When a model must predict 100 things and does each with 10% error, small errors in each multiply into big errors overall. But when predicting one thing carefully, all learning capacity targets that one stream. Neighbor sensors provide context (this machine usually heats up when temperature rises) without added complexity.
910.po: Evaluation on industrial sensor data shows 1.7 to 7.5 times higher anomaly detection accuracy than methods predicting multiple streams. The simple idea of 'one target plus its neighbors' dramatically improves practical anomaly detection.

911.bp: Extracting information from text—finding person names, organizations, event types—requires understanding both the language and how information maps to predefined categories. But every company uses different category definitions. Training a model on one company's categories makes it forget another company's.
911.wh: The 'schema alignment tax' is the cost of learning multiple schemas: if you train a model on both Company A's event types and Company B's different event types, the model often loses ability on both because the definitions conflict. For example, Company A's 'hiring' event differs from Company B's 'promotion' event.
911.ap: The paper proposes separating the task into three phases. Phase 1: The large language model learns to find entity and event spans (the raw information) across all companies' data at once, ignoring categories. Phase 2: The model assigns semantic concepts to each span ('this looks like a hiring event' as a concept, not a category). Phase 3: Small, lightweight models map these concepts to each company's unique schema.
911.ww: This works because finding spans is universal (everyone writes names and events the same way in text), but mapping to categories is company-specific. By separating general ability (span finding and conceptualization) from category mapping, the large model doesn't have to memorize conflicting definitions. Lightweight models easily handle company-specific mappings.
911.po: The method avoids the performance drop that normally happens when training on multiple schemas, and the first two phases are reusable for any new company. It shows that schema-agnostic information extraction outperforms direct schema-dependent approaches.

912.bp: Named entity recognition—identifying names of people, places, organizations in text—requires labeled training data, which is expensive to collect. Self-training is a method where you train on labeled data, then use the model to label more data, then retrain. But the model often makes mistakes on its own unlabeled data, and then learns from its mistakes.
912.wh: Confirmation bias is the core problem: if the model confidently labels something wrong, it reinforces that wrong belief in the next training round. You need a way to filter out high-confidence mistakes before they corrupt the learning process.
912.ap: The paper proposes using a large language model as a judge. After the main model generates predictions on unlabeled data, they prompt the LLM to evaluate whether each prediction looks correct, using prompts that encode task-specific rules (mined from the labeled data). They then blend the main model's confidence with the LLM's judgment, and apply probability smoothing to reduce overconfident predictions.
912.ww: This works because large language models have broad knowledge of entity types and can spot incoherent predictions (e.g., 'the date March 15 is a person name' is obviously wrong). Their judgment breaks confirmation bias. Blending multiple confidence signals and smoothing reduces the risk that any single signal dominates. The prompts built from labeled rules give the LLM task-specific guidance.
912.po: The method outperforms other self-training approaches on multiple named entity recognition benchmarks. It shows that leveraging an LLM's broad knowledge as a filter makes self-training practical and reliable.

913.bp: When you ask a large language model 'What is the capital of France?', a retrieval-augmented system first retrieves relevant documents (Wikipedia article on France), then asks the model to generate an answer using those documents. This is more reliable than pure generation because the model can cite sources.
913.wh: Real-world knowledge comes in many forms: tables (census data), graphs (social networks, knowledge bases), trees (documents with sections), unstructured text. Each form requires different handling—you can't treat a table the same as free text. Also, retrieving wrong information is dangerous in high-stakes settings (medical advice, financial decisions).
913.ap: The paper is a tutorial (not a research paper) that surveys retrieval-augmented systems from a structural perspective. It reviews how different knowledge structures (tables, graphs, text) require different retrieval and generation strategies, covers the full pipeline from indexing through generation, and addresses safety concerns like adversarial retrieval and misuse prevention.
913.ww: This works as a teaching resource because structure matters deeply. A table query needs different retrieval than a text query. A graph requires link traversal. By teaching the structural perspective, practitioners can design retrieval systems appropriate to their data type, rather than treating all external knowledge the same.
913.po: The tutorial provides a unified framework for understanding retrieval-augmented systems across their full lifecycle and different knowledge structures, plus guidance on safety. It helps practitioners choose the right approach for their data type.

914.bp: Matrix deflation is a mathematical technique where you decompose a matrix into layers (rank-1 pieces), subtracting each layer one by one until the matrix is empty. It's useful for image compression, dimensionality reduction, and data analysis. Traditionally, a human decides when to stop (usually when the remaining noise is small enough).
914.wh: Deciding when to stop is arbitrary—thresholds like 'stop when remaining norm is 10% of original' are human guesses. For noisy data, the norm might never reach 10%, or it might hit 10% before extracting the real signal. You need an adaptive decision, not a fixed threshold.
914.ap: The paper proposes an agent-based approach: a large language model generates proposed rank-1 layers (singular value decompositions), and a vision model looks at the intermediate result and decides 'does this layer look meaningful? should we continue?'. The vision model replaces the numeric threshold. They improve the language model's output by permuting rows/columns to expose cleaner visual structure.
914.ww: This works because visual judgment can detect signal without math. A human can look at a partially deflated image and say 'this looks like half of a digit, keep going' or 'this is just noise, stop.' By teaching a vision model to make this judgment, you replace threshold-hunting with learned pattern recognition. In-context learning lets the language model see good examples and refine accordingly.
914.po: On synthetic data where the true rank is known, the agent achieves deflation within 1.75 units of the target. On real image data, it matches traditional numerical results while adapting thresholds dynamically, showing that agentic, threshold-free deflation is viable.
